newsitem.title: UK: Prompt Brent leaps, output cut in N.Sea, US Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Prompt Brent leaps, output cut in N.Sea, US Gulf.

text.p: The prompt North Sea Brent market surged higher on Friday, but traders differed over whether the move was backed by bullish underlying fundamentals despite production cuts on both sides of the Atlantic.

The August/September Brent intermonth spread traded early and +10 cents, but swiftly headed further into backwardation to change hands at a high of +19 cents with a European major dominating the buying.
"The spread is really steaming but there's only one buyer in the market," said one trader.
September/October also firmed to trade at -6 cents and itself was on the brink of backwardation by midday.
Outright levels for September Brent slipped, and the contract was trading 11 cents down at $18.58 a barrel at 1228 GMT.
Physical Brent was untraded but two Norwegian grades were traded at levels close to deals on Thursday.
An Oseberg loading August 17-19 fetched Dated Brent +29 cents, while an August 11-13 Ekofisk moved at Dated Brent +25 cents.
Five Brents from early in the August programme were due to turn wet on Friday.

An unexpected cut back in production at the North Sea Nelson field, which feeds into the Forties stream, was offering the market a short-term boost, as were storm-related production shut-ins in the Gulf of Mexico, traders said.
Nelson operator Enterprise Oil said that likely to be cut back by around 60,000 barrels per day on Friday until the middle of next week due to problems with the gas system.
A spokesman said production was currently running about 10,000 bpd down at 130,000 bpd, but needed to be cut to around 70,000 bpd to prevent excess gas flaring.
Forties equity holders and buyers said that they had not yet been given a clear indication of changes to the July loading programme, but most expected cargoes to be deferred rather than cancelled.
"We have bought cargoes and are expecting to see some deferrals rather than actual cancellations... but as a customer we're waiting for clarification," said one trader.

Traders were also eyeing possible sales to U.S. Gulf refiners which have dealing with a supply short-fall after tropical storms forced rig evacuations in the Gulf of Mexico and Colombia's Cano Limon field was shut-in after a pipeline was sabotaged.
But others said demand in the U.S. Gulf would be easily covered by West African barrels and suggested the jump in August values was geared towards lifting profits on swaps positions.
"The fundamentals just aren't there for a big jump in the market. It's manipulation linked to whatever positions these guys have got," said one North Sea trader.
